claims.claim: egg production from the Rose et al. 1999 model (via Rose et al. 2001), the denominator of the project's ~0.04–0.09 % egg-to-15-October survival
claims.conditions: simulated yellow perch egg production, no. eggs/ha (×10⁻⁶ in the table's unit, i.e. 0.80, 1.11 and 1.35 million eggs/ha), for decreased, baseline and increased egg mortality. Each is the mean over the last 35 years of a 50-year individual-based simulation of Oneida Lake, not a field count
claims.note: The input checks (baseline 1.11 × 10⁶ eggs/ha = 111 eggs/m²). The numerator is VanDeValk et al. 2023's 15-October count, which I did not read. With the field figures in the project's notes (950/ha long-term, 825/ha in 2022), the ratio is 0.07–0.09 % (950/1.11 M = 0.086 %; 825/1.35 M = 0.061 %). The lower bound of ~0.04 % is not reproduced from those, so check it against VanDeValk. Cite Rose et al. 1999 Table 9 directly; the 'via Rose et al. 2001' is not needed. The model's own egg-to-age-2 survival is 210/1.11 M ≈ 0.019 %.

claims.claim: halving or raising egg mortality changed first feeders 4.4-fold but age-2 recruits by only about 8 % (205, 210 and 221 per hectare) (Rose et al. 1999, via Rose et al. 2001)
claims.location: p. 148 (PDF p. 22), Table 9 (page image read); egg mortality rates p. 139 (PDF p. 13)
claims.quote: Lower total number of first feeders … 178 325 … 85 036 … 40 894
claims.conditions: model predictions, means over the last 35 of 50 simulated years. Baseline egg mortality 0.11/d (10 % egg survival), decreased to 0.06/d (29 %) and increased to 0.15/d (4 %). Recruitment = abundance at age 2

claims.claim: the share mature at age 4 rose from 24 % (low egg mortality) to 54 % (high), through lower perch density
claims.location: p. 148 (PDF p. 22), Table 9 and Discussion ('Density dependence')
claims.quote: which led to density-dependent yellow perch growth and maturation
claims.conditions: Table 9 'Younger maturation, percent (age-4)': 24, 41, 54 for decreased, baseline and increased egg mortality
claims.note: The mechanism is fewer young perch, which means less walleye predation, faster growth of the young and of adults, and earlier maturation. Adult abundance stayed nearly the same (103, 106, 112/ha), so 'lower perch density' means lower density of young perch, not of adults.

tried.note: redirects to an HTML application page (17 characters of text), not the PDF

notes: Also in Table 9 (decreased / baseline / increased egg mortality): 18-mm abundance 60,594 / 30,329 / 15,325 per ha; survival 18 mm → age 2 0.41 / 0.85 / 1.56 %; age-4 length 205 / 215 / 221 mm; eggs per spawner 27,885 / 30,313 / 30,989; spawners 29.1 / 35.4 / 44.2 per ha. Adult walleye fell from 20.2 to 19.9 to 16.1 per ha with rising perch egg mortality (p. 142). Walleye responded differently (Table 10): rising egg mortality was not fully compensated, so recruitment and adult abundance declined. The model sets a floor on egg mortality of 0.015/d (at 14 °C) and caps yolk-sac larval mortality at 0.09/d (at 12 °C) (p. 131).
